front.title: Multicast Dispatch for the Secure Reliable Transport Protocol

abstract.t: This document describes the experimental multicast dispatch profile implemented in Robotweax SRT 0.3.2. One sender transmits shared DATA over IP multicast while maintaining per-receiver unicast control and repair sessions. This initial editorial draft records the wire representation and identifies unresolved protocol and deployment requirements.

section.name: Status and Scope
section.t: This is an unsubmitted editorial draft. The organizational author and document name are placeholders. It is not a complete independently implementable specification. Statements describing version 0.3.2 are implementation observations, not IETF consensus. Open issues are intentional and must be resolved or explicitly scoped before claiming conformance.

The baseline is Robotweax SRT commit 235cbdb6c0b0d1950b3e74d623ffc21108bf3ef1. This profile uses Live Message Caller/Listener connections. Packet-filter FEC, File/Stream and Rendezvous are excluded. IPv4 multicast has documented sample qualification; an IPv6 encoding is not evidence of IPv6 deployment qualification.

section.name: Transport Model
section.t: The Listener is the sole DATA sender. Each Caller receiver has a unicast session for admission, acknowledgments, negative acknowledgments, key exchange and repairs. Original DATA is emitted once to the multicast destination. Every original and repair names the dispatch group in the DATA destination-socket field, including unicast repairs. The receiver routes both paths into one member reliability state.

Membership uses group type 4, reserved for multicast in the base SRT draft. Use of that value does not imply allocation of the additional handshake extension. The receiver accepts multicast DATA only for the announced group identity and sender source. Source filtering is not cryptographic sender authentication.

Each receiver retains its own control and repair state. The sender remains open without receivers, and accepted sends advance the group position without delivery. Initial joining position, timestamp mapping and retained-history boundaries require complete serial-arithmetic definitions; see Open Issues.

section.name: Dispatch Handshake Record
section.t: The Listener CONCLUSION carries CONFIG extension type 0x7f14. This provisional value is not an IANA allocation. Content is exactly 60 bytes, excluding the normal four-byte extension header; its length is 15 four-byte words. Integers use network byte order.

Offsets and widths: 0/4 magic 0x52574d01; 4/4 dispatch group ID; 8/1 address family (4 or 6); 9/1 flags; 10/2 destination UDP port; 12/16 multicast address; 28/16 interface selector; 44/4 initial sequence; 48/8 signed timestamp-origin delta in microseconds; 56/1 hop limit; 57/3 reserved zero.

Flag bit 0 indicates an interface hint; other bits are zero. IPv4 addresses occupy the first four bytes of address slots and the remaining bytes are zero. For IPv6, the interface-selector slot contains twelve zero bytes followed by a 32-bit scope index. With no hint, the entire selector is zero. A local receiver interface override takes precedence; an index is host-local and its cross-host meaning remains an open issue.

The implementation rejects wrong length or magic, unknown family/flags, nonzero reserved/padding bytes, a non-multicast destination, port zero, an initial sequence above 0x7fffffff, and invalid group/interface identity. The group-ID mask and its relationship to SRT socket identifiers require a portable definition. Duplicate records and unsupported combinations must be included in the conformance corpus.

section.name: Delivery and Repairs
section.t: Unicast repair is the default. With a configured threshold of 1 through 16 distinct requesting receivers, a bounded per-sequence tally can cause one multicast repair for shared loss. Suppression begins only after local UDP acceptance. A repeated request by the same receiver uses unicast, permitting recovery if the multicast repair was lost. Transient multicast send failure falls back to unicast.

The current implementation uses a tally window described as a couple of round trips. A normative formula, expiration rules, capacity/eviction rules and duplicate-request handling remain to be specified from code and tests. This draft does not turn that informal description into a requirement.

The elected transmitting member must accept a message before suppressed members commit it. Backpressure does not advance the group sequence. Per-member bandwidth caps constrain the elected multicast transmitter and individual repairs; there is no separate aggregate cap. A network-suitable aggregate feedback and repair policy remains unresolved.

section.name: Shared Traffic Keys
section.t: Each receiver has its own key exchange and key-encrypting context, but the sender shares one traffic-key schedule and salt across the dispatch group. Admission requires matching encryption mode and key length. A receiver starts participating only after initial group-key confirmation. A dispatch receiver does not retain the ordinary handshake key clone as an alternate DATA key.

Rotations follow consumed group sequence positions, including receiver-free intervals. Members preannounce successor keys separately. Rotation is positional rather than waiting for all receivers to acknowledge; a receiver missing a key leaves affected DATA unacknowledged and may recover through unicast repair within its latency budget. The implementation retains four generations for repairs.

CTR and GCM use sequence-based IV derivation. A repeated packet reuses its protected representation, with the GCM retransmission bit normalized for AAD. The same key and nonce must not protect different plaintext/header inputs. A complete extended-position/generation algorithm, wrap vectors, key-retention boundary and failure-atomicity rules are still required.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: Shared keys permit admitted receivers to forge traffic authentic under the group key. AES-GCM therefore does not establish sender identity against group insiders; AES-CTR does not provide DATA integrity. Source-address filtering does not fix either limitation.

Leaving does not revoke learned keys; admission does not guarantee that a joiner cannot decrypt retained historical ciphertext protected by its newly learned keys. There is no per-receiver forward/backward access guarantee. Deployments must treat the group as one trusted domain unless a future version supplies stronger protection.

Review must cover handshake tampering, redirection to multicast destinations, unauthorized membership, feedback amplification, receiver state exhaustion, forged control traffic, congestion and denial of service. An implementation source review is not independent cryptographic or network-scale qualification.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: No allocation request is made in this initial editorial version. Type 0x7f14 is a provisional implementation value; no private-use reservation is asserted. Before publication, coordinate the extension namespace and group-type semantics, decide an allocation policy and specify migration if a collision is found.

section.name: Open Issues
section.t: Define full admission/retry and receiver lifecycle state machines, timestamp-origin mapping, serial arithmetic, extended generation positions, cipher interactions, key-generation failure and repair retention. Produce independent wire vectors for IPv4/IPv6 encodings, rollover, late joining and empty-group progression.

Decide aggregate congestion and feedback policy, slow-receiver handling, supported multicast deployment scope, interface-hint semantics and combinations with authentication extensions. Qualify physical network behavior separately from loopback media tests. A second independent implementation is desirable maturity evidence.
